title: How a white blood cell decides what is a threat
question: How does a white blood cell know what to attack?
representation: Follow one neutrophil through contact, two candidate surfaces, a receptor match, a zoom into the PAMP molecule, the response, and the resulting rule. Branches open the PAMP detail from the comparison beat.

example.title: A neutrophil meeting a bacterium and a self cell
example.description: One immune cell, two surfaces, one receptor match.

branches.reason: Opening the PAMP spike: lipid A anchor and sugar chain

chapters.title: Contact is not yet a decision
chapters.question: What does a neutrophil actually check when it touches something?
chapters.insight: Contact is necessary but not sufficient.
chapters.safeguard: Avoid the reading that any collision triggers an attack.
chapters.narration: A neutrophil patrols with receptors on its surface. Touching a cell tells it almost nothing. The decision starts when one of those receptors matches a molecular pattern on the surface it has touched.

roles.neutrophil: Neutrophil: First responder. It patrols tissue and tests surfaces with membrane receptors.
roles.receptors: Surface receptors: Y-shaped probes. Each has a shape that can bind one family of molecules.
roles.environment: Tissue space: Self cells and microbes are both present. Contact alone cannot separate them.

cues.text: A neutrophil patrols with receptors on its surface.
Touching a cell tells it almost nothing; the receptor match is the test.

presentation.why: Establishes which part of the cell makes the decision, before any candidate appears.
presentation.visualEvidence: Membrane receptors sample the surface; contact alone carries no verdict.

continuity.bridge: Opening beat: establish the question and the actor.

chapters.title: Two candidates at once
chapters.question: Which of these two surfaces should the cell attack?
chapters.safeguard: Do not equate 'foreign-looking' with 'dangerous' without the receptor match.
chapters.narration: A bacterium carrying PAMP spikes and a self cell carrying MHC-I markers arrive together. The bacterium is a threat; the self cell is the body's own tissue. The cell has to tell them apart while both are in contact range.

roles.bacterium: Bacterium: Carries PAMPs: molecular patterns found on microbes but not on host cells.
roles.self_cell: Self cell: Displays MHC-I markers that identify it as the body's own tissue.

cues.text: A bacterium with PAMP spikes and a self cell with MHC-I arrive together.
The self cell is not a threat, even in contact range.

nodes.title: Bacterium
nodes.body: Carries PAMPs: molecular patterns found on microbes but not on host cells.

nodes.title: Self cell
nodes.body: Displays MHC-I markers that identify it as the body's own tissue.

visual.takeaway: Danger and self can arrive together; the cell must distinguish them.

presentation.why: Puts the two candidate surfaces side by side at the moment of decision.
presentation.visualEvidence: One surface carries PAMPs, the other carries self markers.

continuity.bridge: The previous beat established that receptors test surfaces. Two surfaces now demand a verdict.

chapters.title: Inside a PAMP spike
chapters.question: What is a PAMP, physically?
chapters.insight: The pattern is chemical shape, not appearance.
chapters.safeguard: Avoid treating PAMPs as invisible tags; they are molecules with a shape.
chapters.narration: A PAMP is a molecular pattern, not a label. On this bacterium the spike is built from lipopolysaccharide: a lipid A anchor in the membrane and a sugar chain projecting outward. The receptor's binding pocket fits that shape, which is why this surface, and not the self cell, is recognised.

roles.pamp: PAMP spike: Lipopolysaccharide: lipid A anchored in the membrane plus a projecting sugar chain.
roles.receptor: Receptor pocket: A shape complementary to the PAMP. Binding is the recognition event.
roles.membrane: Bacterial membrane: Holds lipid A in place; the sugar chain is what the receptor actually contacts.

cues.text: A PAMP is a molecular pattern, not a label.
Lipid A anchors the spike; the sugar chain is what the receptor contacts.

nodes.title: PAMP spike
nodes.body: Lipid A anchors it in the membrane; the sugar chain is what the receptor contacts.

nodes.title: Receptor pocket
nodes.body: A shape complementary to the PAMP. Binding is the recognition event.

nodes.title: Bacterial membrane
nodes.body: Holds lipid A in place; the sugar chain is what the receptor actually contacts.

visual.takeaway: A PAMP is a molecular shape the receptor can bind, not a warning label.

presentation.why: The learner asked what the spike is, so the branch resolves its molecular construction.
presentation.visualEvidence: The spike decomposes into a membrane anchor and a sugar chain that fits the receptor.

continuity.bridge: The comparison showed two surfaces; this beat opens one of them to explain what the matching pattern actually is.

chapters.title: From match to response
chapters.question: What does the cell do after the match?
chapters.insight: Recognition and response are separate steps.
chapters.safeguard: Do not imply the cell 'knows' the bacterium is harmful beyond the pattern match.
chapters.narration: Binding starts a signal cascade that reaches the nucleus. The cell extends pseudopodia, pulls the bacterium inside, and digests it in a phagosome. Cytokines then leave the cell and recruit more neutrophils to the site.

roles.signal: Signal cascade: Surface binding becomes an internal signal reaching the nucleus.
roles.engulf: Engulfment: Pseudopodia wrap the bacterium into a phagosome.
roles.digest: Digestion: An oxidative burst destroys the bacterium inside the vesicle.
roles.recruit: Recruitment: Cytokines call more neutrophils to the tissue.

cues.text: Binding starts a signal cascade that reaches the nucleus.
Cytokines leave the cell and recruit more neutrophils.

continuity.bridge: The detail beat explained the match; this beat follows what that match sets in motion.

chapters.title: The decision rule
chapters.question: What should we remember?
chapters.safeguard: Do not reduce immunity to a single receptor; this is one innate recognition path.
chapters.narration: PAMP match, attack. Self marker, ignore. The immune decision is specificity of recognition, not the fact of contact.

roles.attack: PAMP match → attack: A receptor binds a microbial pattern, so the response starts.
roles.ignore: Self marker → ignore: MHC-I identifies host tissue, so no response is started.

cues.text: PAMP match, attack. Self marker, ignore.
The decision is specificity of recognition, not contact.

nodes.title: PAMP match → attack
nodes.body: A receptor binds a microbial pattern, so the response starts.

nodes.title: Self marker → ignore
nodes.body: MHC-I identifies host tissue, so no response is started.

visual.takeaway: Recognition specificity, not contact, decides the response.

presentation.why: Condenses the lesson into the two outcomes the learner must keep.
presentation.visualEvidence: The same contact event produces opposite outcomes depending on the match.

continuity.bridge: The mechanism is complete; this beat compresses it into a rule to remember.
